8306_JP_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Japan's largest bank and one of the largest financial institutions in world. Holds ~8.4% of all domestic loans and 11.8% of deposits in Japan as of March 2025, making it the largest non-Chinese bank group globally, with a balance sheet slightly larger than those of JPM and HSBC. Headquartered in Tokyo and with over 360 years of history, MUFG has a global network with over 2,700 locations in more than 50 countries and over 180,000 employees. One-stop financial supermarket: if you're a Japanese salaryman opening a savings account, a mid-size Japanese company getting a business loan, a multinational corporation doing a billion-dollar bond issuance, or a pension fund looking for asset management, MUFG likely has a product for you. 7 segments: Digital Services, Retail & Commercial Banking, Japanese Corporate & Investment Banking, Global Commercial Banking, Asset Management & Investor Services, Global Corporate & Investment Banking, and Global Markets. the Japanese bank with the largest exposure to overseas operations. Japan accounts for ~50% of total profit. Banking in Thailand and Indonesia contributes ~15%, and equity-method earnings from Morgan Stanley make up most of the rest. MUFG and Morgan Stanley announced a definitive agreement on September 29, 2008, under which MUFG would invest $9bn in equity in Morgan Stanley for a 21% interest on a fully diluted basis. The structure was: $3bn for 9.9% of common stock at $25.25 per share, and $6bn of perpetual non-cumulative convertible preferred stock with a 10% dividend and a conversion price of $31.25 per share. ~22% stake in Morgan Stanley has contributed 25%+ of earnings in each of the past five years
8306_JP_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: Rate Normalization Tailwind: After decades of near-zero interest rates destroying Japanese bank profitability, the Bank of Japan has finally begun normalizing rates. Even modest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan dramatically expands MUFG's net interest income given its enormous deposit base and domestic loan books. Massively Undervalued vs. Global Peers: MUFG's valuation remains subdued relative to the earnings power that higher ROE would imply, suggesting the market has not fully priced in the impact of rate normalization and digital efficiency gains. Shareholder Returns Improving:  MUFG is returning excess aggressively, ¥500 bn share buyback in 2025 plus ¥74 per share in divs, a 40% payout ratio directly addressing the long-standing critique that Japanese banks retain too much equity. Morgan Stanley Stake: ~20 stake provides earnings exposure to U.S. investment banking and wealth management — a high-quality, recurring earnings contributor. Southeast Asia Growth Platform: MUFG has meaningful ownership in fast-growing emerging market banks in Thailand, Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines.  Has retained large positions in Southeast Asian banks including a major stake in Bank of Danamon in Indonesia and Krungsri in Thailand
8766_JP_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Japan's first insurance company founded in 1879, providing marine insurance to support Japan's burgeoning international trade. Today, over 50,000 employees in more than 40 countries work toward the realization of its purpose. The company offers a wide range of insurance and related services including non-life insurance, life insurance, reinsurance, asset management, risk management, health and wellness services, and financial services, covering sectors such as agriculture, aviation, marine, energy, and life sciences. It also generates income from fee-based services (risk management consulting, asset management) through its Financial & General segment, but this is a smaller contributor.
8766_JP_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: Consistent compounder: TM has delivered ~20% EPS CAGR over the past 5 years. 13+ consecutive years of dividend growth: DPS have increased every year since 2011, with a 50% payout ratio policy. Disciplined underwriting: Combined ratios in North America have averaged 90-91%, the underwriting business generates profit before even counting investment income. Capital release story: Japan's regulators and governance reforms are pushing companies to unwind "cross-shareholdings" (the old practice of Japanese companies owning each other's stock). Tokio Marine is sitting on ~¥2.5 trillion (~UDS $17bn) in these holdings, a massive, multi-year capital return/M&A war chest. Berkshire Hathaway endorsement:On March 24, 2026, Berkshire's National Indemnity Company announced a $1.8 billion (¥287.4bn) strategic stake, with plans to collaborate on reinsurance and global M&A Global diversification at a reasonable valuation: Despite its scale and quality, trades at a discount to Western insurance peers.

Why he left: He didn't really "leave". It was a standard Japanese corporate succession. In June 2025, Komiya stepped down as Group CEO and assumed the position of Group Chairman. He continues to focus on developing future leaders and serves as Dean of the Tokio Marine Group Leadership Institute, which he founded in April 2023. ASML_NA_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION:What started as a failing joint venture between ASM International and Philips in a leaky shed, widely dismissed even by the engineers who worked there, ASML eventually became the sole supplier of one of the most critical tools in the entire global semiconductor supply chain.ASML is a capital equipment company with a dominant position in deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography machines and sole manufacturer of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machines. Lithography machines are tools used by chipmakers like TSMC, Samsung and Intel to manufacture the world’s most advanced chips. While the business mix is diversified by region, system and technology, the customer base is highly concentrated, with TSMC and Samsung representing 38% of total sales in 2025 (24% and 14%, respectively). Geographically, sales are split between China (41%), Taiwan (36%), Korea (35%) and the US (18%) with the balance in Japan, EMEA and the rest of Asia. By system, half of sales are generated from DUV machines and half are generated from EUV machines. 25% of total sales are install base management, which is essentially their aftermarket and servicing business. This includes maintenance and field service (ASML technicians are often embedded at customer fabs for regular upkeep), software upgrades, hardware (physical) upgrades and parts and consumables (for components that need to be replaced over time). Services grow as the install base grows, are recurring in nature, are less cyclical and provide a floor during downturns.
ASML_NA_Equity|growth_algorithm: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: At the 2024 investor day, management guided to €44-60bn in sales by 2030, implying 6-13% annual growth from 2025 levels. They target 56-60% gross margin by 2030, mostly the result of mix shift to higher margin EUV products. With margin expansion and share buybacks, EPS should grow 20%+, and with the dividend, total shareholder return should be slightly higher.
ASML_NA_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: The most advanced modern technology does not exist without ASML. Fundamentals are strong with sales growing low-teens, operating margin 35% and growing, solid free cash flow (margin 34%) and net cash on the balance sheet. Secular growth tailwinds trump short-term cyclicality in this trillion dollar market: Chips are the building blocks for the digital economy. They are pervasive, powering everything from smartphones and computers to datacenters, cars and medical devices. Global semiconductor sales have grown mid-single-digits annually for decades to $800bn in 2025, expected to top $1tn this year. Wafer fabrication equipment sales (including lithography machines) have grown high-single-digits annually since the late 1980s, with acceleration in recent years (5-year CAGR is 15.8%). WFE is high-teens as a percent of global semi sales (and growing), and lithography represents 25-30% of total WFE spend (and growing). Monopoly in EUV lithography with an impregnable moat:ASML dominates its part of the value chain, with 90% of the DUV lithography market and 100% of EUV. The other two competitors in DUV are Nikon and Canon. ASML benefits from a system of interlocking barriers that make its position nearly impossible to replicate. Their technology is the embodiment of accumulated engineering knowledge across hundreds of interdependent subsystems (laser physics, vacuum engineering, mirror optics, etc.) which took decades of effort and significant resources to master. Switching costs are high (in time in and in money) as they co-develop technology roadmaps with customers who have each invested billions into integration. The services component deepens their already entrenched customer relationships.
ASML_NA_Equity|management: Management and capital allocation: President and CEO Christophe Fouquet joined ASML in 2008 and held several management positions in marketing and product management prior to CEO, including Chief Business Officer from 2022 to 2024, EVP of EUV from 2018 to 2022 and EVP of Applications from 2013 to 2018. Prior to ASML, he worked at industry peers KLA Tencor and Applied Materials. Executives are long-tenured with decades of accumulated technical knowledge. While CFO Roger Dassen comes from a pure finance and audit background (previously at Deloitte), there are mostly engineers at the top (the CEO has a physics background, and the CTO is a mathematician). On capital allocation, the hierarchy follows a fairly classic framework for a capital-light, high-margin industrial business. Priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business, with R&D treated as sacrosanct and cap ex spend to scale production capacity, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. Over the last three decades, they’ve spent nearly €34bn on a cumulative basis on R&D, which is consistently low- to mid-teens as a percent of total sales. This spend is not discretionary, but rather the engine that sustains the monopoly. Since the mid-1990s, ASML has spent nearly €15bn on cap ex on a cumulative basis (typically mid- to high-single-digits as a percent of sales) to ensure sufficient manufacturing capacity to build enough machines to meet demand. ASML has returned €16.7bn in dividends over the last two decades, and they’ve repurchased €28.2bn in stock over that same time frame. Nearly 75% of buybacks have occurred in the last five years. While M&A is not a priority, ASML has made selective, strategic acquisitions over time, mostly to internalize critical technology dependencies (for example, acquiring Cymer for their industry leading laser light sources).
ASML_NA_Equity|negatives: Negatives - Shares fell 3.8% following the print despite the beat-and-raise, reflecting the demanding scale of the implied second-half ramp and unresolved China policy risk. First-half 2026 free cash flow was negative (€1.3B) despite €5.7B of net income over the same period, as inventory and prepayments built ahead of the H2 shipment ramp. The raised full-year guidance implies €14B+ of net sales in Q4 2026 alone, an unusually demanding execution requirement in a single quarter. EUV fell to 57% of system sales in Q2 (from 66% in Q1) as DUV/immersion (29%) and metrology gained share. Not necessarily negative, but a reminder that near-term mix will swing quarter to quarter. A small number of customers (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, and memory makers) continue to account for the large majority of sales (roughly 61% from the top four customers in 2025).
ASML_NA_Equity|positives: Positives - Total net sales of €9.3B were above the €8.4-9.0B guided range, up 21% year-over-year (€7.7B in Q2 2025) and 6% sequentially (€8.8B in Q1 2026). Gross margin of 54% exceeded the 51-53% guided range. Net income rose 26% year-over-year to €2.9B (basic EPS of €7.59). Installed Base Management (service) sales of €2.76B came in roughly €300M above guidance, underscoring a high-margin, recurring revenue engine that management expects to grow >30% annually. Full-year 2026 outlook lifted to €43- 45B net sales and 54-56% gross margin, the second upward revision in 2026. Intel Foundry reached a production milestone using High-NA EUV on its 18A process for Core Ultra Series 3 chips, which is the first concrete commercial validation of the platform. Management said ASML has “already received substantially all orders needed for 2027 and a large number of orders for 2028,” a multi-year demand signal well beyond the normal order book. On capital returns, the interim dividend was raised to €1.88/share (from €1.60 in the prior interim), plus €1.1B of share buybacks in the quarter.
ASML_NA_Equity|special_items: Special items: ASMLhas granted a “stichting”, or preference share option, to a Dutch foundation established under Netherlands law that acts as a poison pill defense mechanism. This protects ASML’s independence and long-term strategic orientation (which is important for a company that sits at the center of global geopolitical contest over semiconductor technology). It also means ordinary shareholders have limited ability to influence change. The Dutch government has also made clear through policy signals that ASML is a strategic national asset, adding another layer of implicit protection beyond the preference share option.

AZN_LN_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: One of the world's largest pharma companies, headquartered in Cambridge, UK focused on several major disease areas: cancer (oncology is the largest (~40% of rev), heart and kidney disease, respiratory conditions like asthma and COPD, and rare diseases. Key products: cancer drug Tagrisso ($7.3bn 2025 rev), cholesterol drug Farxiga ($8.4bn), COVID-19 vaccine developed with Oxford University. Stated goal to deliver $80bn in total rev by 2030 (vs $58.7bn in 2025) via growth in its existing oncology, biopharma, and rare disease portfolio, and by launching 20 new medicines. Oncology (~40% of rev): Largest, fastest-growing segment. Generated $24bn in 2025, +17% y-o-y. Key drugs include Tagrisso (lung cancer), Imfinzi (lung, liver, biliary cancers), Enhertu (HER2 cancers, ADC), Lynparza (ovarian, breast, prostate), and Calquence (blood cancers). Cardio, Renal & Metabolism(~22% of rev): Key drugs include Farxiga/Forxiga (heart failure, kidney disease, diabetes), Brilinta (heart attack prevention — now in decline due to generics), Lokelma (potassium management), and Roxadustat. Vaccines & Immune Therapies: Primarily consists of legacy COVID-19 vaccine rev (now largely wound down) and Beyfortus (RSV prevention in infants), developed with Sanofi. Emerging Markets: EM outside China grew 22% in 2025, and geographic expansion — particularly in Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East — is a structural part of the growth story. Long-term themes include market expansion in emerging regions alongside transitions to advanced modalities like cell therapies and immune engagers.
AZN_LN_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: Size + Growth: ANZ is not just a dividend vehicle like many big pharmas. Rev grew 8% in FY2025, with core EPS up 11%. Execution record: CEO Pascal Soriot set a $45 billion rev target a decade ago and hit it. He then set the $80 bn target. The management team has delivered 16 positive Phase III readouts in the past year alone. Track records of pipeline execution are rare and worth paying for. The $80 bn by 2030 target assumes significant growth in the existing oncology, biopharmaceuticals, and rare disease portfolio, and by launching an expected 20 new medicines before the end of the decade. Strong pipeline: Broad portfolio of over 100 ongoing Phase III trials and over 20 late- stage readouts slated for 2026. CEO called this an "unprecedented catalyst-rich period.” Mgmt has noted they've already achieved 10 of the 20 new medicines targeted as part of the 2030 roadmap. EM growth driver: EM ex-China grew 22% in 2025. As healthcare systems in Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East develop, AZN is well-positioned with an established commercial footprint in these regions. This could be a decades long tailwind Rare disease is high-margin: 2021 Alexion acq gave AZN a leading position in complement biology (treating ultra-rare diseases). These drugs face almost no generic competition, have high prices, & have loyal patient populations. Rare Disease grew 15% in Q1 2026.
AZN_LN_Equity|management: MANAGEMENT: Sir Pascal Soriot CEO Sir Pascal Soriot is one of the most consequential pharmaceutical executives of his generation, a French-born Australian businessman who took over a British-Swedish pharma giant in crisis, rebuilt it into one of the world's most scientifically ambitious and commercially dynamic life sciences companies, and delivered one of the most remarkable corporate turnarounds of the twenty-first century.
AZN_LN_Equity|negatives: OTHER NEGATIVES: Debt Load from Alexion Acquisition: The $39 bn Alexion deal in 2021 left the balance sheet leveraged. While net debt has been declining, AstraZeneca still carries meaningful d+ebt, which constrains financial flexibility and leaves it more exposed to interest rate environments than a net- cash pharma peer like Roche. ADC Platform Concentration: ADCs are a competitive space with Pfizer, Roche, and others investing heavily. If the platform disappoints, or a competitor leapfrogs AstraZeneca's technology, the growth premium embedded in the stock erodes quickly.
AZN_LN_Equity|positives: OTHER POSITIVES: Leadership in Antibody-Drug Conjugates (ADCs): ADCs are a new generation of cancer drugs that deliver chemotherapy precisely to tumor cells. AZN, through its partnership with Daiichi Sankyo, is a clear leader. Enhertu achieved sales growth of 34% on a constant exchange rate basis in Q1 2026. The ADC platform has multiple drugs in development across different cancer types, giving it a multi-year runway. Oncology Dominance with Room to Expand: Oncology generates $25.6 bn, 44% of product revenue, growing at 17%. The key drugs — Tagrisso, Imfinzi, Enhertu, Calquence — are each expanding into new cancer types and earlier treatment lines, meaning the addressable market for drugs already approved keeps growing without needing new approvals. Operating Leverage: AZN is targeting mid-30s core operating margins, and Core EPS is consistently growing faster than rev. Progressive Dividend + Buyback Optionality: Modest yield (~2%), but the dividend has never been cut, and as the debt from the Alexion acq is paid down, there is increasing potential for capital returns to accelerate (divs or share repo)
BABA_US_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: Alibaba is China's version of Amazon, Google Cloud, PayPal, and eBay all rolled into one. It is the biggest e-commerce company in the world by gross merchandise volume (GMV) and operates online shopping platforms including Tmall, Taobao, Alibaba.com, AliExpress, and Lazada. Beyond shopping, it runs a cloud computing business, a logistics network, digital media, and is pushing into A.I. Headquartered in Hangzhou, China. Founded in 1999 by Jack Ma. Alibaba doesn’t make things, it runs platforms that connect buyers and sellers and takes fees, ads, and services revenue. Four Segments: 1. China E-commerce (~52% of rev): The heart of the company. Includes Taobao, Tmall, the B2B platform 1688, and food delivery service Ele.me. Forecast to generate around CN¥565 billion in 2026. Taobao is like a giant online flea market where anyone can sell. Tmall is like a premium digital mall for established brands. Makes money through seller advertising, transaction fees, merchant services 2. International Digital Commerce (~13 of rev): Replicating the China marketplace globally. Includes AliExpress and Lazada (Southeast Asia), Trendyol (Turkey), Daraz (South Asia), with a strategic focus on key regions including select European markets and the Gulf Region. Growing fast but still small. 3. Cloud Intelligence (~12% of rev): BABA’s version of AWS, cloud computing and AI services for businesses. Provides computing, data storage, AI services, enterprise software. Rev grew 26% y-o-y, driven by public cloud rev growth and the increasing adoption of AI-related products. Cloud and AI are among Alibaba’s fastest-growing areas. 4. All Others: Freshippo supermarkets, Cainiao (logistics network that coordinates warehouses, delivery partners, cross-border shipping helping merchants deliver goods faster), Alibaba Health, mapping app Amap, and digital media assets. Most of these businesses are still losing money but improving.
BABA_US_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: AI and Cloud accelerating: Alibaba Cloud achieved double-digit rev growth in FY 2025, with AI-related product rev growing more than 100% for seven consecutive quarters positioning BABA as China's answer to AWS or Azure. Largest cloud provider in China. Massive AI investment signals long-term ambition: Plans to invest more than $50bn into AI infra over the next three years. Beijing has shifted from foe to ally: Gov has signaled renewed support for its domestic tech champions via regulatory softening and public encouragement of private sector innovation, a big shift from the crackdown era. Shareholder returns: Share repo authorization of $19.1bn as of Sep 30, 2025 Core e-commerce has stabilized: Showed clear signs of stabilization in 2025, with e-commerce customer management rev returning to 10% growth after years of concern that Taobao and Tmall were in structural decline. Exposure to China Consumer: China has ~1.4 bn people, a huge middle class and a massive e-commerce market historically dominated by Alibaba. Massive E-commerce Ecosystem: Alibaba’s platforms connect: hundreds of millions of consumers with millions of merchants

BBSE3_BZ_Equity|investment_thesis_summar: INVESTMENT THESIS: Strong moat: Exclusive distribution through Banco do Brasil's ~4,000 branches under an agreement running to 2033 Capital-light: brokerage arm converts that access into commission income with minimal capital and ROEs in the stratosphere. BP/_LN_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: BP is one of the world’s largest oil and gas companies, founded in 1908 as the Anglo-Persian Oil Company. BP finds oil and gas, extracts it, ships it around the world, refines it into fuel, and sells it to consumers and businesses. BP has operations in 61 countries, produced ~2.4 mm barrels per day of oil equivalent, and had total proven reserves of over 6bn barrels. BP also runs around 21,200 service stations worldwide under the BP, Amoco (US), and Aral (Germany) brands. 2025 replacement ratio increased to 90% from 50%. BP earns through three interlocking mechanisms. 1) sells crude oil and nat gas at market prices (highly sensitive to the Brent crude oil price and European/US natural gas benchmarks). 2) earns a refining margin — the spread between what it pays for crude and what it receives for refined products like petrol, diesel, and jet fuel. 3) earns retail and services income from Castrol lubricants, aviation fueling, and convenience stores. Geographical breakdown: BP's upstream production is split roughly 40% US, 25% Middle East, 15% North Sea (UK/Europe), and 20% Asia-Pacific. The US is the single largest geography through BPX Energy (shale) and Gulf of America operations. BP has committed to growing US production to approximately 1mm boe/d by decade's end. Dividend: Div cut 50% in 2020 during COVID, a significant trust-breaking event for income investors. The dividend has been rebuilt since but has not returned to pre-2020 levels. Buyback: BP suspended buybacks in 2025 to focus on debt reduction. It will resume once net debt hits the $14–18 bn target range 3 segments: Oil Production & Operations (~60% of 2025 EBIT): Crude oil exploration and production, including BPX Energy (its US shale business), operations in the Gulf of America, the UAE, and the North Sea. Upstream remains dominant at ~70% of FCF generation Gas & Low Carbon Energy (~9.5% of 2025 EBIT): Natural gas production, LNG trading, offshore and onshore wind, solar, hydrogen, and carbon capture. Customers & Products (~29% of 2025 EBIT): the downstream business — the 21,200 petrol forecourts, Castrol lubricants, refining operations, oil trading, EV charging, and aviation fueling.
BP/_LN_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: Turnaround story: Growing upstream oil and gas production; focusing the downstream business by reshaping the portfolio around advantaged integrated positions; and disciplined, capital-light investment in biogas, biofuels, and EV charging. sec Cost reduction is also a major lever — BP has achieved $1.7bn in structural cost reductions, on track to meet or exceed its goal of $4–5bn by end-2027. $20 billion asset sale program: Divestments will generate cash that can be used to cut debt, fund buybacks, and grow the dividend. Commodity leverage: BP offers leveraged exposure to oil and gas prices. New CEO optionality: O'Neill has a track record of bold, value-creating restructuring at Woodside. If she can apply the same formula to BP, the upside could be significant. Depressed valuation: BP trades at a meaningful discount to Shell, ExxonMobil, and Chevron on most metrics. Significant re-rating potential. High dividend: ~5.5% yield is attractive particularly with a stated commitment to grow the dividend 4%+ annually. Elliott's presence: Having one of the world's most sophisticated activist investors as the 2nd-largest shareholder looking for value creation is a meaningful catalyst.
BP/_LN_Equity|management: Management/Board The company just went through its fourth CEO change in six years. BP's board appointed Meg O'Neill as CEO, effective April 1, 2026. Murray Auchincloss stepped down in December 2025. O'Neill is BP's fourth CEO since 2020 and its first external hire for the role in more than a century. She is the first woman to lead a top-five oil major.  The 55-year-old executive transitions from Australia's Woodside Energy, where she held the CEO position starting in 2021. Her career includes a 23-year tenure at Exxon Mobil prior to joining Woodside. During her tenure at Woodside, she orchestrated a merger with BHP's petroleum division, creating a top-10 independent global oil and gas producer with a $40bn valuation, and successfully doubled Woodside's production capacity. She is known for financial discipline, LNG conviction, and bold strategic moves. As O'Neill takes over, she benefits from a war-driven surge in prices — but inherits what observers describe as the industry's toughest cleanup job, including a mountain of debt, an organizational structure many believe is too sprawling, and a portfolio cluttered with low-return units. Her predecessor Murray Auchincloss was a 30-year BP insider who had served as CFO before becoming CEO. He reversed BP's disastrous overreach into renewables under Bernard Looney but was ultimately replaced before finishing that turnaround.

IMB_LN_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION: 4th largest international tobacco company, located in Bristol, UK. The turnaround, which includes restoring wholesale channel partner relationships, clearing excess inventory and refreshing the product lineup should result in a return to profitable growth. Secular trends favorable in a massive and fragmented market: Increasing participation in sports and fitness activity drives demand for performance-oriented footwear and athletic apparel. This is even more notable in emerging markets like China and other parts of southeast Asia where disposable incomes are rising. Increasing chronic disease is also leading to government investment in sports infrastructure more broadly. Athleisure (performance gear becoming part of everyday wear) also drives demand. On a combined basis (athletic footwear and apparel), the market is sized at $500bn, growing mid-single-digits annually. The market is even larger if you expand to include all athleisure. Leading brand in athletic footwear and apparel with a strong and defensible moat: In a highly fragmented market, Nike is a standout. It is multiples larger than most peers, with the exception of adidas. Nike benefits from tremendous scale (they spend $4bn on demand creation annually) which gives the company a distribution advantage as well, namely with wholesale channel partners that need Nike on their shelves. When you’re the dominant brand in athletic footwear, you’re too important for any major retailer to drop. Nike’s brand is consistently ranked among the most valuable brands globally, alongside companies like Apple and Coca Cola. Its brand is one of the most culturally embedded and globally recognized, which gives the company sustained pricing power.

Hill started at Nike in 1988 as an intern, working his way up to oversee all commercial and marketing operations for Nike and the Jordan brand. Capital allocation priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business, mostly through demand creation and product innovation, and more recently through supply chain restructuring and rebuilding wholesale relationships, and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through the dividend and opportunistic share repurchases. Nike is not acquisitive. The dividend is treated as sacrosanct, as they’ve raised the dividend for 24 consecutive years, despite recent operational challenges. Since 1995, Nike has paid out $23bn+ in dividends, and they’ve repurchased $53bn+ in shares. They’ve reduced the pace of buybacks in recent years due to the ongoing turnaround, but management is likely to pick up the pace following a return to more profitable growth.

QXO_US_Equity|why_we_own: Why we own QXO is Brad Jacobs' latest industry roll-up, this time targeting building products distribution, the network of businesses that moves roofing, insulation, siding, and other construction materials from manufacturers to contractors and jobsites. Following the Beacon Roofing (2025), Kodiak Building Partners (April 2026), and TopBuild (July 2026) acquisitions, QXO operates roughly 1,150 locations across all 50 states and seven Canadian provinces, more than 10,000 delivery vehicles, and 28,000 employees, generating combined annualized revenue of $18bn+. The company holds the no. 1 position in insulation and waterproofing distribution and no. 2 in roofing distribution, making it the second largest publicly traded building products distributor in North America. QXO doesn't manufacture anything. Like Jacobs' prior roll-ups (United Waste Systems, United Rentals, XPO/GXO/RXO), it owns the distribution and logistics layer connecting a concentrated set of manufacturers to a highly fragmented, relationship-driven base of contractors and builders. The building materials distribution market spans $800bn across North America and Europe combined (QXO's own stated North American TAM, where it currently operates, is $300bn), growing an estimated 5-9% annually through 2031, and remains extraordinarily fragmented. An estimated 10,000 distributors compete across North America alone, most of them small, family-run operations without QXO's scale, owned logistics fleet, or balance sheet. That fragmentation, combined with a purchasing process that is inherently relationship- and trust-based and hard to digitize or centralize quickly, is the same setup Jacobs has exploited three times before. Buy the scale advantages smaller competitors can't match (national account relationships, owned last-mile logistics, procurement leverage), then layer in technology (an integrated ERP, warehouse management, and pricing platform are targeted for 2027) to extract efficiency the fragmented incumbents never had the capital to build. Management's stated long-term targets are to more than double EBITDA by 2030 and reach $50bn of revenue within the decade, a bar Jacobs has hit or exceeded in each prior roll- up, albeit on a much longer timeline than the 2+ years QXO has operated so far. QXO is not yet the free-cash-flow generator we typically own, and QXO's negative cash generation is structural to a company still mid-build. Leverage roughly doubled over the past year to fund Kodiak and TopBuild, and the balance sheet will carry that debt through several more quarters of integration before any targeted margin expansion shows up. The bull case here isn't "proven moat generating cash today", it's a bet that Jacobs' repeatable playbook plays out a fourth time in a new but structurally similar industry. On current evidence, QXO belongs in PFOE as a higher-risk position underwritten on execution and the Jacobs track record, not yet as a demonstrated-quality, FCF-generative core holding.

V_US_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION:Visa is the largest processor of debit and credit transactions globally, operating as a "toll booth" for global commerce. They connect consumers, banks and merchants, making commerce safer, faster and more reliable for all parties. Specifically, the company facilitates authorization, clearing and settlement of payment transactions and delivers related products and services, including engagement solutions, risk and security services, and consulting and advisory solutions. They do not issue credit or lend money, but collect a small fee based on volume and number of transactions processed. The total monetary volume of all transactions processed through the network is $16.7tn annually and growing at a mid- to high-single-digit rate. The number of individual transactions routed through the network for authorization, clearing and settlement is 310bn+ annually, growing at a high-single-digit to low-double-digit rate. They’ve spent the last few decades building out the merchant acceptance network, which is north of 175mn (and when you include digital endpoints, it expands the network’s reach into the billions of individual accounts and real-time payment rails). The business is diversified across segments and geographies. 36% of sales are derived from data processing, 25% from international transactions, 32% from services, and the remaining 7% from other sources (advisory services, licensing fees and the like). From a regional standpoint, 39% of sales are generated in the US with 61% from international markets. There are 5bn+ Visa-branded cards in circulation (and growing at a mid- to high-single-digit clip).

V_US_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: Despite an ever-evolving payments landscape, most roads lead back to Visa and Mastercard payment rails. Fundamentals remain strong with sales growing low-double-digits, operating margin modestly expanding, solid free cash flow (margin 50%+) and manageable leverage (net debt to free cash flow < 1x). Multiple tailwinds driving growth in a large and attractive market: Visa sizes the opportunity at $240tn+ annually in global payment volumes. Core PCE represents $41tn of the TAM (excluding China), with an even larger opportunity in non-core commercial and new payment flows. These include $145tn in business-to-business payments and $55tn in peer-to-peer, business-to-consumer and government-to- consumer payments. Services TAM is $520bn+ (in dollars, not payment flows). The largest services opportunities include advisory services, risk & security, issuing and acceptance solutions. Tailwinds driving growth include growth in global PCE (mid- single-digits), the continued secular shift from cash and check to digital forms of payment (low- to mid-single-digits), acceptance growth and e-commerce. Duopoly in global payments with one of the most unassailable moats in existence: Outside of China, Visa (no. 1) and Mastercard (no. 2) operate a global duopoly. Visa benefits from global scale, strong network effects and a solid brand. They enable transactions for customers through the network in 200+ countries, and with 5bn+ Visa branded cards and 175mn+ points of acceptance, Visa products and infrastructure are truly ubiquitous. While Visa and Mastercard dominate carded payment flows in global PCE (excluding China), cash, check and ACH remain their largest competitor, with global PCE card penetration at 2/3 of total payments.
V_US_Equity|management: Management and capital allocation: CEO Ryan McInerney, age 49, has been with Visa since 2013. Prior to the CEO role in 2023, he served as President of Visa’s global businesses. Before joining Visa, he served as CEO of consumer banking at JPMorgan Chase, and before that, he was a principal at McKinsey in the firm’s retail banking and payments practices. CFO Chris Suh, age 54, joined Visa in 2023 from Electronic Arts where he served as CFO. Prior to EA, he held senior finance roles at Microsoft for nearly two decades, most recently as CFO of the cloud and AI division. The most consistent thread in executive backgrounds prior to joining Visa is major financial institutions and strategy consulting (particularly JPMorgan and McKinsey), with big tech as a secondary feeder. In short, management is long-tenured and deeply domain specialized. Capital allocation priorities include 1) reinvesting back into the business for future growth (organic and inorganic) and 2) returning excess capital to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks. Strategic M&A is disciplined and bolt-on in nature. Notable acquisitions include Visa Europe for $24bn in 2016, Earthport for $320mn in 2019 (cross-border payment capabilities), Tink for $2.2bn in 2022 (open banking), Currencycloud for $963mn in 2022 (cross-border payment capabilities), and Pismo for $1bn in 2024 (enabled connectivity for emerging payment rails like Pix in Brazil). Since the IPO in 2008, Visa has paid out $33.2bn in dividends and they’ve repurchased $138bn in shares outstanding. They’ve increased the dividend every year since March 2008 and current yield is 0.9%.
V_US_Equity|special_items: Special items: Visa has a complex share structure as a result of the company’s origins as a member cooperative. Class A common stock is the public float that has ordinary voting rights (one vote per share). Class B common stock is held by US member banks. These shares were issued at the IPO at US financial institutions that were members of Visa USA before the reorganization in 2008. They are not publicly traded and carry transfer rights tied to litigation resolution. These shareholders retain exposure to pre-IPO interchange litigation. Each time Visa puts money into escrow to settle that litigation, it effectively reduces the Class A shares that Class B shareholders will eventually receive (so they bear the litigation cost, not public shareholders). Class C common stock is held by non-US member institutions with a conversion rate of four to one (one Class C converts into four Class A upon transfer). They also have preferred stock created specifically for the 2016 Visa Europe acquisition. These are convertible into Class A but the conversion rates on certain of these shares can also be reduced to offset liabilities from litigation relating to multilateral interchange fee rates in the Visa Europe territory.

WDAY_US_Equity|company_description: COMPANY DESCRIPTION:Workday is a cloud-native enterprise application software company with roots in enterprise resource planning, or ERP. Specifically, they sell mission-critical products and services in human capital management, or HCM, and financial management systems, or FMS. As a software-as-a-service, or SaaS company, Workday sells subscriptions in-cloud (average terms not disclosed but minimum duration is three years) with major feature releases delivered twice a year, and weekly, smaller feature updates delivered with minimal downtime disruption. Feature releases are not subject to additional fees. The business mix is roughly 75% HCM and 25% financials, with the latter growing faster than the former (low-20s versus mid-teens over the last few years). From a geographic standpoint, the US represents 75% of total sales with the balance OUS. The company’s subscription backlog, or remaining performance obligations, which represents total contractual commitments for services that will be performed in the future, topped $27bn in the most recent period, up from less than $4bn in fiscal 2017. They currently serve 11,500 customers, including 65% of the Fortune 500 and have 80mn+ users generating 1.4tn transactions globally. Gross retention rate, which indicates stickiness of the existing customer base (and excludes upsell), consistently exceeds 95% with churn mostly due to M&A. Net retention (including upsell) is north of 100%.
WDAY_US_Equity|growth_algorithm: Long-term growth algorithm and expected return: Expect low-teens sales growth driven by growth in new customers or “logos” (going down market to medium enterprise and capitalizing on the larger opportunity OUS) as well as cross-sell and upsell to existing customers. With margin expansion and opportunistic share buybacks, EPS should grow mid-teens. There could be additional upside to total shareholder return if the multiple re-rates.
WDAY_US_Equity|investment_thesis_summary: INVESTMENT THESIS: Fundamentals are solid with sales growing low-teens, operating margin improvement, strong free cash flow and net cash on the balance sheet. Multiple favorable trends in a large and growing market:While no longer early days, ERP workload migration from on-premise to cloud remains a tailwind. A structural shift to unified, single platform systems of record benefits vendors like Workday compared with stitching together point solutions. AI is also (currently) a tailwind to growth. The opportunity is estimated at nearly $200bn, with > 50% of the regional opportunity in markets OUS and > 50% of the vertical opportunity in financials versus core HCM. The opportunity has expanded over time as Workday expands the product portfolio into non-core adjacencies like payroll, talent management (recruiting, reskilling), workforce planning and analytics in HCM and financial planning (budgeting, forecasting), procurement and spend management in FINS. Gold standard in HCM software (contender in FINS) with a historically strong moat: Workdayoffers thegold standard in HCM software, particularly for large enterprise. They’ve been named a leader in Gartner’s magic quadrant for cloud HCM suites for 1,000+ employees for 10 consecutive years, competing mostly with Oracle and SAP. In financials, they have consistently gained market share and have also been recognized by Gartner as a magic quadrant leader (shorter duration than HCM). Workday benefits from high switching costs, scale and distribution advantages in a market still mid-migration (from on-premise to cloud), proprietary data feeding the AI layer, and a unified system of record. Customer captivity is evidenced by 95%+ gross retention revenue, as it’s painful to rip and replace mission-critical software. With HR and finance on one unified platform, AI agents get richer context with people and money data living in one graph as opposed to being stitched together across systems.
WDAY_US_Equity|management: Management and capital allocation: CEO Aneel Bhusri co-founded the business with Dave Duffield in 2005 and served as sole or co-CEO from 2009 to 2024. Before Workday, he held several leadership roles at PeopleSoft, including vice chair of the board and senior vice president responsible for prod uct strategy, business development, and marketing. PeopleSoft (acquired by Oracle in 2005) is an on-premise enterprise software company that provides HR, finance and other back office applications. Bhusri holds an MBA from Stanford and a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and economics from Brown University. Note that after stepping down as co-CEO in 2024, naming Carl Eschenbach sole CEO at the time, he returned earlier this year to “lead in the rapidly evolving AI era”. There was a gap between the official messaging and how it was received externally, though I personally view it as a net positive. Much of the rest of the management team has been freshly reassembled. Both the Chief Commercial Officer and President of Product and Technology have decades of experience at Google and SAP. CFO Zane Rowe was appointed in 2023 with ties to former CEO Carl Eschenbach, which makes him a bit of a continuity figure though his tenure is short. On capital allocation, priorities include reinvesting back into the business, strategic M&A and returning excess capital to shareholders through buybacks. While declining as a percent of total sales (currently high-20s), R&D remains a priority. Workday has spent $6.3bn on acquisitions over the last decade+. Notable deals include Adaptive Insights for $1.5bn in 2018 (enhanced financial planning, budgeting and forecasting), Scout RFP for $500mn in 2019 (cloud- based procurement), Peakon for $700mn in 2021 (real-time visibility into employee experience) and VNDLY, also in 2021 (cloud-based external workforce and vendor management company). The earlier era of M&A helped the company build out the product suite, particularly in non-core financials, whereas the current era is focused on building out AI capabilities and functionality. Recent notable acquisitions include HiredScore (AI recruiting and talent matching), Evisort (contract intelligence for legal and procurement), Flowise (low-code AI agent building platform), Paradox (conversational AI for frontline/hourly worker recruiting) and Sana (AI native learning and agent platform). Sana was largest with a $1.1bn price tag. Over the last few years, Workday has repurchased $4.1bn+ in shares, offsetting share dilution from stock-based compensation. In September 2025, the board authorized an additional $4bn in repurchases. They’ve targeted a total of $5bn in repurchases through the end of fiscal 2027, which should more than offset SBC.
